title: Class activation mapping
summary:
Class activation mapping (CAM) methods are explainable AI techniques used to visualize the regions of an input image that are the most relevant for a particular task, especially image classification, in convolutional neural networks (CNNs). These methods generate heatmaps by weighting the feature maps from a convolutional layer according to their relevance to the target class.

CNNs are a specific architecture of deep learning models designed to process spatially structured data such as images, exploiting a series of convolution, non-linear activation, and pooling operations to extract relevant features. CNNs and deep learning models more broadly are described as black boxes due to their complex and non-transparent internal layers of representation. The need for clearer indications on internal working and decision-making processes gave birth to explainable AI techniques.

Class activation mapping was the original version of CAM methods, firstly introduced by Zhou et al. in their seminal work "Learning Deep Features for Discriminative Localization." This approach achieves class-specific heatmaps by modifying image classification CNN architectures, replacing fully-connected layers with convolutional layers and a final global average pooling layer. Gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) is a generalized version of CAM that tackles its architectural limitations. Grad-CAM computes the gradient of a target class score with respect to the feature maps of a convolutional neural network. The main advantage of Grad-CAM is that it is model agnostic, meaning it generates visual explanations for any CNN-based network without architectural changes or re-training.

More advanced versions of these methods are not limited to image classification tasks but have been extended to several vision-related tasks, such as object detection, image captioning, visual question answering, and image segmentation.
